name: Homebase
subcategory: HR, recruiting, payroll and workforce operations
tagline: Build staff schedules and time-off workflows without payroll or hiring services

tiers.name: Basic
tiers.limits: 1 location; up to 10 employees; 90 days of timesheet history

tiers.name: Essentials
tiers.limits: Per location; unlimited employees; 4+ years of timesheet history; scheduling, time tracking, and team communication

tiers.name: Plus
tiers.limits: Per location; unlimited employees; adds labor-cost controls, time-off/PTO, and permissions

tiers.name: All-in-One
tiers.limits: Per location; unlimited employees; adds onboarding, HR/compliance tools, and advanced controls

pricing.freeTierCaps: 1 location; 10 employees; 90 days of timesheet history
pricing.billingTerms: free + monthly/annual paid plans (annual rates are 20% lower); 14-day All-in-One trial
pricing.hiddenCosts: Pricing is per location, not per company. Add-ons include Payroll $39/month+$6 per paid employee, Tip Manager $25/location/month, background checks $30, Task Manager $13/location/month, job boosts $79/post, and Hiring Assistant $30/post.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Homebase, build staff schedules and time-off workflows without payroll or hiring services. The hard boundary is time clocks, payroll, messaging, labor-law tools, hiring, and support, plus compliance, payroll, and regulated integrations.
coreLoopDIY: Build staff schedules and time-off workflows, maintain approvals and records, and export data without payroll calculation, hiring services, or employment decisions.
whatYouLose: time clocks, payroll, messaging, labor-law tools, hiring, and support
identity checks and global employment infrastructure
ongoingBurden: sensitive data, access, retention, audit, payroll calculations, filings, benefits, employment law, incident response, and support
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Homebase because HR platforms survive because mistakes affect pay, benefits, immigration, and legal obligations, not because forms are difficult to render. The recurring cost buys sensitive data, access, retention, audit, payroll calculations, filings, benefits, employment law, incident response, and support, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Frappe HR
priorArt.desc: Active open-source human-resources and payroll application built on Frappe.

alternatives.name: Sling Free
alternatives.desc: Shift scheduling, availability and swaps for 30 people; the time clock is where the upsell starts.

facts.install: Hosted signup, then invite employees by email or phone to the web, iOS and Android apps
facts.dataFormat: Schedules, availability, requests and messages in Sling's cloud account; schedules and many records export as CSV or XLS
facts.gapVsPaid: The free plan schedules up to thirty users but withholds the time clock and labor-cost tools that make Homebase useful to hourly teams.

alternatives.name: 7shifts Comp
alternatives.desc: Schedules, availability, time off and shift swaps for one 15-person location; restaurant branding comes free too.

facts.install: Hosted signup for one restaurant location, then invite staff to the web and mobile apps
facts.dataFormat: Employee profiles, schedules, availability, time-off and communications in 7shifts' cloud, with selected reports and export tools
facts.gapVsPaid: It is limited to one fifteen-person restaurant location and keeps time-clock and more advanced operations features outside the free tier.

alternatives.name: Connecteam Small Business Plan
alternatives.desc: Scheduling, time off and shift changes for ten people; user eleven has a price tag.

facts.install: Hosted signup, then invite staff to the web and mobile apps
facts.dataFormat: Employee records, documents, schedules and time data in Connecteam's cloud; schedules and timesheets export to Excel, PDF, CSV or payroll-specific files
facts.gapVsPaid: The free plan ends at ten users, below many shift teams, and its broader operations suite is less scheduling-focused than Homebase.

alternatives.name: Horilla HR
alternatives.desc: Schedules, rotating shifts and leave in Docker; a whole HR suite comes along for the ride.

facts.install: Clone the stable 2.0 branch and run docker-compose up -d; a manual Django setup is also documented
facts.dataFormat: HR records in PostgreSQL by default, with uploaded media on server storage or optional Google Cloud Storage
facts.gapVsPaid: A whole self-hosted HR system is substantially harder to administer and less friendly to frontline schedulers than Homebase.
facts.setupBlocker: Docker and production configuration: database credentials, secret key, allowed hosts, HTTPS, backups and mail remain the operator's job

alternatives.name: Frappe HR
alternatives.desc: Schedules, shifts and leave in a full HR stack; running the stack is the unpaid role.

facts.install: Launch its Docker Compose stack, or install hrms and ERPNext into an existing Frappe Bench
facts.dataFormat: Each Frappe site has its own MariaDB database plus private/public files directories; backups are SQL dumps and file archives under the site
facts.gapVsPaid: It can model shifts and leave, but the full Frappe stack is far more operational work than Homebase's managed scheduler.
facts.setupBlocker: The full Frappe/ERPNext stack brings Docker, MariaDB, Redis, proxy/TLS and version-compatible app upgrades

rejectedAlternatives.name: Homebase Basic
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The $0 plan builds a weekly schedule, but availability, time-off requests and shift trades start on paid tiers.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Jibble Scheduling
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The free scheduling page still says Coming soon, so it cannot replace a scheduler today.

rejectedAlternatives.name: TimeTrex Community
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Community Edition was discontinued in October 2024 and no longer receives security updates.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Essentials plan and a internal records tracker without payroll DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Homebase in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: build staff schedules and time-off workflows, maintain approvals and records, and export data without payroll calculation, hiring services, or employment decisions.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement employees, teams, roles, documents, leave requests, equipment, onboarding tasks, and acknowledgements.
Use least-privilege roles and log every read or change to sensitive records.
Add approval workflows, expiry reminders, export, retention, deletion holds, and encrypted backups.
Keep compensation fields optional and never calculate payroll, taxes, benefits, or statutory filings.
Provide a data dictionary and explain which fields should not be stored without legal review.
Ship Docker Compose, health checks, disaster recovery, and an emergency-access procedure.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out payroll calculation or money movement.
Deliberately leave out automated hiring decisions or applicant scoring.
Deliberately leave out tax, benefits, immigration, identity, and global-employment compliance.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
